So long, white marble shower. Designers are going big on bathrooms with serious Milanese swagger, including moody stones in green or oxblood, walnut paneling, and Art Deco fixtures channeling iconic architect Piero Portaluppi
The dominance of the gray-and-white “spa bathroom” may be waning. You know the ones—spare, mostly white, flooded with light, and sheathed in acres of Calacatta Viola marble. The new look involves dramatically veined stone in dark green or dusky red, sculptural Art Deco–style fixtures, and rich woodwork. Think: the bathrooms of AD cover stars like interior designer Athena Calderone and supermodel Paloma Elsesser. The reference point is 1930s Milan, where bold material combinations and precise geometry turned these utilitarian spaces into showpieces.
Few designers are as identified with this look as Piero Portaluppi (1888–1967), the Rationalist architect behind the iconic Villa Necchi Campiglio and Casa Corbellini-Wassermann. While his dramatic entry halls and sweeping stairs have inspired designers for decades, it’s the rooms with plumbing that are currently having a moment.
At Villa Necchi, mirrored walls multiply the swirling patterns of Arabescato Orobico marble, while at nearby Casa Corbellini-Wassermann, Portaluppi set vibrant green Verde Challant marble against graphic black stonework. “He frequently used contrasting materials to frame hallways, thresholds, and architectural elements, allowing these moments of juxtaposition to draw the eye and bring a sense of ceremony to the space,” explains Calderone, who visited Villa Necchi with architect Danielle Siggerud while reimagining her own Tribeca apartment.
AD100 designer Gregory Rockwell says he is drawn to Portaluppi's unconventional palette. “What I love about Portaluppi is how controlled everything is architecturally, but then he’ll do something extravagant with the marble or an unexpected color,” the designer says. For the primary bathroom of Elsesser’s Brooklyn town house, Rockwell and colleague Hester Hodde layered burgundy Rosso Francia marble, walnut-and-mirror paneling, and pistachio-green walls. “It’s a slightly strange combination when you think about it, but I love the colors together,” he says.
For Calderone, the magic is in the stonework. “There was such ingenuity in the way Portaluppi clad entire bathrooms in stone, often using smaller, individually composed pieces,” she says. For her primary bathroom, she edged sweeping expanses of pale stone with intricate inlaid tile borders and added Art Deco–inflected fixtures and geometric mirrors. Looking back at Portaluppi’s examples, she observes: “It feels almost at odds with how we approach stone today, where expansive, perfectly bookmatched slabs have become the prevailing ideal. He embraced the irregularity and variation in the veining.” That appreciation for the individuality of natural stone is also on display in her own powder room, which features a pedestal sink in deeply veined Verde Alpi marble.
Another sink in the same deep-green stone can be found in the powder room of a Milan pied-à-terre Giampiero Tagliaferri recently designed for a young art collector. “The custom pedestal sink takes its bold, geometric form from Rationalist architecture, but we kept the lines clean and the layout modern,” Tagliaferri says. As the designer explains, revisiting 1930s Milan isn’t about exactly replicating a Portaluppi bathroom. “Reinterpretation is about extracting a period’s core DNA, not literal replication.”
That thinking extends beyond bespoke interiors. New bath collections are borrowing from the Portaluppi bathroom vocabulary, offering ways to incorporate patterned stone, geometric forms, and saturated color without a full-scale renovation. Artistic Tile’s Calacatta Gold marble mosaic brings the intricacy of Calderone’s inlaid borders to walls and floors, while Kelly Wearstler’s oxblood-hued Treillage tile for Ann Sacks puts a dimensional spin on the burgundy tones of Elsesser’s bathroom. For Clé Tile, Reath Design created marbleized patterns that evoke the movement of natural stone. The influence extends to smaller details: Charles Edwards’s alabaster dish light has an Art Deco–inspired silhouette, while Crate & Barrel’s Verde Green marble soap pump and tissue holder bring the distinctive color and veining of those Verde Alpi sinks down to countertop scale.
Whether it’s an entire room wrapped in marble or a single well-chosen detail, the impulse is much the same. “I’ve never really understood why bathrooms should be any less interesting than the rest of the house,” Rockwell says. “They might as well be beautiful and exciting.”

The commercial cost of extreme heat and drought: How the 2026 summer hit horticulture
From lost sales and delayed projects to rising costs and changing customer behaviour, the summer of 2026 has exposed the commercial consequences of extreme heat and drought for horticulture.
The summer of 2026 has brought into sharp focus the challenges of operating in an increasingly extreme climate. Across horticulture, businesses have had to contend with rising temperatures, prolonged dry conditions, disrupted trading patterns and pressure on infrastructure. From nurseries and garden centres to landscapers and visitor attractions, the effects have extended beyond the immediate challenge of managing plants through heat and drought to affect sales, costs, investment and the wider supply chain.
This five-part series examines how the summer’s extreme heat and prolonged dry conditions are affecting horticulture, from the immediate commercial consequences for businesses to the longer-term challenges facing the industry. This first article looks at sales, customer behaviour, stock-holding costs and the wider supply chain. The second turns to working conditions, employee health and productivity. The series then examines the effects on plants and production, the growing pressure on water security, and what the industry needs to do to prepare for a hotter future.
A summer of extremes
Temperatures reached 35°C or higher in every month from May to August. By mid-August, the UK had already recorded 35 days of 30°C or above somewhere in the country, breaking the previous annual record of 34.
Speaking at Horticulture, The Conference, meteorologist Laura Tobin described extreme heat as the “new normal”. Climate models presented by Tobin indicate that, under medium-emissions scenarios, UK summer temperatures could regularly reach the low 30s°C in the north and up to 40°C in the south by mid-century.
Prolonged low rainfall, combined with high temperatures that increased evaporation and water demand, accelerated the development of what the Environment Agency described as a “flash drought”. England and Wales recorded their driest July in 190 years, with England receiving just 7% of its long-term average rainfall during the month and parts of south-east England receiving only 1%. By August, 71.3% of England was officially in drought, with more than 27 million people subject to water-use restrictions.
The scale of the dry conditions has since become clearer. On 16 October, the Government declared severe drought in parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. The South East and South West experienced their driest April-to-September period in more than a century. Environment Agency modelling indicates that England needs 120% of typical rainfall between September 2026 and April 2027 to recover fully from drought, underlining the risk that its effects will continue into the next growing season.
With temperatures falling and rain returning, it would be easy to forget that the summer of 2026 ever happened. But the severe drought declaration is a reminder that it is far from over, and that its effects will reach well into the next growing season.
For horticulture, the lessons of this summer cannot be allowed to fade with the heat. The sector needs to act on them now, before the next heatwave arrives, and prepare for conditions that will increasingly disrupt production, sales and investment.
Extreme heat: Economic, business and social risk
The wider economic implications of extreme heat are becoming increasingly clear. Heatwaves can disrupt businesses and supply chains, increase operating costs and compound other risks, including drought and water scarcity.
The human cost is just as stark. Heat is the UK’s deadliest climate-related health risk: estimated heat-related deaths in England from the May and June heatwaves alone nearly matched the record total for the whole of 2022. Its effects fall hardest on the most vulnerable, and reach across communities, public services and the places where people live and work.
The National Heat Risk Commission (NHRC), established in March 2026 to examine the UK’s preparedness for rising temperatures, has highlighted the scale and interconnected nature of these risks in its report, A Heat Circuit Breaker for the UK, published by the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics.
The Commission is chaired by Emma Howard Boyd, former Chair of the Environment Agency for England and Chair of the London Climate Resilience Review.
The Commission’s starting point is that the problem is not a lack of evidence. Its report notes that heat risk has been documented for over a decade, and that statutory advisers, parliamentary committees, researchers and practitioners have made numerous well-evidenced recommendations to address it. Yet those recommendations have not been turned into action. The report highlights 10 that remain unimplemented, spanning governance, people and communities, the built environment and infrastructure, and the economy. “The evidence base is not the main problem,” says Howard Boyd. “The gap is between knowing what needs to change and having the systems, responsibilities, resources and incentives in place to deliver it.”
“The key question is no longer simply what the risks are, but what needs to happen, who needs to act, by when, and what policies, investment, responsibilities and capabilities are required to make that happen,” said Howard Boyd.
She argues that heat cuts across multiple parts of the economy and public sector, including agriculture and food production, water, energy, transport, buildings, infrastructure, businesses and the environment. It can also interact with drought, wildfire and other pressures, making clear ownership and coordination particularly important.
Horticulture sits where many of those pressures meet. It depends on water, energy and transport, on plants that must be kept alive through the heat, and on customers whose confidence rises and falls with the weather. When heat and drought strike together, they do not hit one part of a business at a time but several at once, and the summer has shown how quickly those interconnected risks translate into commercial pressure.
Nursery stock: watering costs, customer confidence and lost sales
For one nursery, the cost of the summer runs to seven figures. Richard McKenna, Managing Director of Provender Nurseries, estimates that the business lost up to £1m in sales over the four months to the end of September as drought and water-restriction messaging discouraged customers from purchasing plants.
For an idea of scale, Provender is a Kent-based wholesale nursery with 75 employees, supplying landscapers, garden designers, landscape architects and retailers nationally. At the time of the interview in September, McKenna estimated that the plant stock on the nursery was worth around £2.7m at cost.
The loss did not come from damaged stock. Concern about whether newly purchased plants could be kept alive during hot weather and water restrictions discouraged customers from buying, with consequences travelling back through the supply chain.
Provender responded with a customer education campaign explaining how to water efficiently and select plants suited to local conditions. But as a national supplier operating across different water company areas, it faced a further complication: restrictions varied by region, making it difficult to give customers consistent advice. McKenna said that even where watering remained permitted, the announcement of a hosepipe ban could be enough to deter plant purchases because customers feared they would not be able to keep them alive.
For growing media businesses such as Melcourt, the timing of dry weather also matters commercially. “As a growing media manufacturer, our peak season is earlier in the year. Early spring droughts affect our sales more than summer droughts,” says Victoria Wright, Technical Manager at Melcourt.
Extreme weather also affects raw materials, but Wright says the industry is used to monitoring its supply chains and mitigating fluctuations before they become a problem. “Whilst extreme weather requires the industry to be more vigilant it doesn’t make it harder to develop peat free growing media.”
Plant sales: shifting seasons and extended stock-holding
Extreme heat and prolonged dry conditions are beginning to alter the traditional sales season for plants and trees. At Provender Nurseries, demand has shifted noticeably, with sales falling away earlier in the year and more stock being carried through the summer as customers become reluctant to plant during periods of heat and water scarcity.
McKenna explained: “May and June have traditionally been very busy sales months for us. But over the past two years, sales have started to fall away in the third week of May, so we’ve lost the final six weeks of the spring and early summer selling season. That means lower revenue and more stock to carry through the summer. Normally, we would run down our stock in July and August, but now we’re holding much more, which costs us more in labour, water and fertiliser to maintain. It also makes the stock we have available in autumn more expensive to produce. With lower revenue, we have less money available to invest. We had planned to spend £50,000 on additional water tanks, but had to defer that investment.”
He still intends to make the investment. “We’ll do it this year, and if we have a good year of sales next year, I’ll invest more.”
McKenna also questions whether the traditional horticultural calendar still reflects the conditions plants are now being asked to establish in. “RHS Chelsea is in the middle of May. Encourages everybody to get gardening, but technically, May is probably a terrible time to plant now because June, July and August are so hot and dry,” he says. “By contrast, September and October can offer more favourable planting conditions with warm soils allowing roots to continue growing well into the autumn.”
He believes the industry is missing the chance to change that message. “If the whole industry made the same noise, saying that if you want your plants to establish and grow better next spring and summer you must plant in September, October and November, that would be amazing. But nobody is shouting about it.”
Some are making the case. In August, the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) urged gardeners to give autumn planting greater importance, arguing that it gives trees, shrubs and perennials time to establish before the following summer and can reduce pressure on water supplies. “Spring may be the season when Britain traditionally gets gardening, but hotter, drier summers mean autumn more than ever also has a crucial role to play,” said Leigh Hunt, Principal Horticultural Advisor at the RHS. The RHS’s own figures show the scale of the shift needed: its plant advice pages received around 13 million views between September and November 2025, compared with around 25 million between March and May 2026.
The wider gardening calendar still leans towards spring. McKenna points out that programmes such as Gardeners’ World go off air for the season just as autumn planting should be promoted, and the flower show season is over.
The effect travels back to the nursery. “Most of our customers are trade, but most of their customers are the end consumer. And that consumer gets their information from Gardeners’ World or the RHS flower shows,” says McKenna. “I had a garden designer here this morning whose client won’t let them plant now, because she thinks the best time to plant is next April or May. He can’t convince her otherwise.”
The result is a squeeze on both margins and investment: nurseries holding stock for longer have less money to spend on the water resilience they increasingly need.
Autumn may offer better planting conditions, but it does not guarantee nurseries a better commercial opportunity.
Like nurseries, garden centres have been under sustained pressure on margins, and many have looked to more lucrative lines to drive sales. Plants are demanding stock to sell: they need daily care, watering and space, and can lose value quickly when conditions turn against them. Over time, many garden centres have broadened their non-plant ranges and, in some cases, reduced the space given to plants.
That shift is most visible at the busiest points of the retail calendar. Halloween and Christmas are now among the most important trading periods for many garden centres. Yet autumn and early winter have traditionally been when nurseries sell their bare-root trees and plants for the planting season, stock that is vital to their year.
Bare-root stock now competes for space and attention with seasonal ranges that are easier to merchandise, sell faster and need none of the care that living plants require. Trees are also a hard sell at that time of year: dormant and leafless, they show little of what they will become. Having already carried stock for longer through the summer, nurseries face a further squeeze if that autumn window narrows too.
Landscaping: delayed projects, tree establishment and aftercare
For Liz Nicholson, Managing Director of Nicholsons, the effects of the drought have been “pretty catastrophic across all landscapes”. Lawns browned off, while soils responded differently according to their composition: sandy soils showed erosion in public spaces, while clay soils developed deep cracks. Nicholson said lawns had since made an 80% recovery, but the full impact on trees would not be clear until the following summer.
Hot, dry weather has affected landscaping businesses in a number of ways, but two stand out: projects have been postponed as clients question whether planting can be sustained, while trees and other plants that do go into the ground need adequate water and aftercare to establish successfully.
David Denny, Director of Research & Knowledge Transfer at the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), said: “The hot and dry weather has had a major impact on the garden landscaping sector. Water restrictions caused many clients to pause the go-ahead with domestic and amenity projects, placing pressure on businesses already grappling with rising costs of doing business.”
The HTA worked with the Association of Professional Landscapers (APL) to provide guidance to members and clients on permitted uses of water, including trickle irrigation and hosepipes for health and safety purposes such as dust suppression.
Denny said the industry’s role was increasingly extending beyond supplying goods and services to helping clients understand how to respond to changing conditions. “Informing and educating clients and the wider public on what water restrictions do and don’t mean is one critical way in which the industry, and especially APL-accredited businesses, are taking on the role of trusted advisor rather than simply a supplier of goods and services.”
Where landscaping projects do go ahead, the survival of newly planted trees and other plants depends on adequate establishment and aftercare, including access to water. This is a particular concern for urban tree planting, where research has highlighted high mortality rates and poor establishment.
Denny said there was growing evidence of trees planted in recent years failing to establish, underlining the need for a more holistic approach to green infrastructure.
A 2025 study by Fund4Trees, which surveyed 687 trees planted across four English cities, found that 21% had died or been removed and only 42% were in good condition. Separate research by the University of Sheffield found that 39% of the trees specified in planting plans across 42 new housing developments were either missing or dead.
“It is vital that tree-planting initiatives incorporate not only the initial funding required for planting, but also funding for establishment programmes, including watering,” said Denny.
Tony Kirkham MBE VMH, former Head of Arboretum, Gardens and Horticulture Services at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, has argued that the industry needs to move from planting trees to growing them. Speaking at the RHS Gardens for our Future summit (2023), he said: “Whatever the reason for species selection we must be successful with the planting, ensuring that we get the operation right followed by good aftercare. Looking after it, watering it, until it’s established and independent.” Kirkham now does all his tree planting in autumn rather than spring, as dry, hot springs increasingly stress newly planted trees.
The risks are particularly acute during periods of extreme heat and drought. During the 2022 drought and heatwave, more than 60% of newly planted trees were severely affected at the worst-hit sites, according to Forest Research.
Denny called for government, town planners and water companies to work with the horticulture industry to ensure that tree-planting initiatives are properly planned and funded, with adequate provision for establishment and aftercare.
Garden centres: heat, footfall and changing demand
For garden centres, the summer’s impact was mixed. Headline trading figures suggest that demand remained relatively resilient, but they mask shifts in what customers were buying, when they visited and how willing they were to invest in gardening.
HTA data showed that sales fell 2% year on year in June, with gardening sales down 5% and customer visits down 2%. July brought a stronger performance, with total sales up 11%, transactions up 6% and average transaction value up 3%. Gardening sales rose 12%, with outdoor living and tools among the stronger categories.
By August, prolonged heat and dry conditions were weighing on core gardening demand. Total garden centre sales were 2% higher than a year earlier, but gardening sales fell 7%, with bedding plants down 11% and hardy plants down 14%. Spending on plant care, garden sundries and tools also fell. Excluding catering, total garden centre sales were down 3%, while catering sales increased 10% and non-garden sales rose 8%. Some spending shifted towards categories less affected by dry conditions: outdoor containers rose 5%, garden furniture 1% and barbecues and heating 2%.
September brought some recovery. Garden centre sales rose 6% year on year, with gardening sales up 11% and hardy plants, shrubs, trees and seeds up 20%, as customers returned to their gardens and warmer-than-average temperatures extended the season. But September typically accounts for just 7% of annual garden centre sales, and gardening sales for the year to the end of September remained 1% behind 2025.
“Gardening sales are still behind last year, showing how difficult it has been to recover the ground lost over the summer,” said Fran Barnes, Chief Executive of the HTA. “A change in the weather does not mean the effects of the extreme conditions have gone away.”
The HTA also highlighted the impact of regional Temporary Use Bans, commonly known as hosepipe bans. Variation in restrictions and weather conditions contributed to differences between retailers, while uncertainty over whether customers would be able to water their gardens made some reluctant to buy plants or commit to larger projects. It mirrors McKenna’s experience at Provender, where regional differences made consistent advice difficult and even the announcement of a hosepipe ban was enough to deter buyers.
Retailers have increasingly taken on an advisory role. Denny says HTA members reported greater interest in drought-tolerant plants, watering products and advice on caring for gardens through prolonged dry periods, with garden retailers advising customers on plants resilient to drought and other climate extremes.
At Yorkshire Garden Centres, Managing Director Mark Farnsworth said the group’s northerly location helped limit the impact of the heat. Nevertheless, watering remained a significant operational challenge, which he described as “relentless”.
The heat also changed how customers used the centres. Some avoided visiting during the hottest parts of the day, while older customers were more likely to stay at home. Restaurants were affected on the hottest days, with some closing early. The group is now considering air conditioning across its restaurants as part of adapting to changing conditions.
Squire’s Garden Centres, which operates 17 centres across the South East, saw a similar shift. “Very simply, when it was extremely hot, footfall dropped as customers were avoiding going out, trying to stay cool,” says Ricky Bowness, Retail Buying Director. Project-led products lost their appeal for a while, with little enthusiasm for “relaying a lawn or putting up a new fence in the weather we were experiencing”. Cooling products for people, homes and pets were in far more demand, and the group’s air-conditioned areas proved popular.
For Bowness, the summer confirmed a longer trend. “Summers over recent years have reinforced that prolonged heat and water scarcity are no longer exceptional,” he says. That is shaping the plant offer: while Squire’s wants to keep a market-leading range, it is focusing on plants that are robust in hot, dry conditions and will review how they are presented so customers can make informed choices. “It all comes back to wanting to make sure that every plant we sell succeeds.”
Heat, in other words, redirects spending as well as suppressing it.
For suppliers, changes in retail demand feed back through the supply chain. “Ultimately, though, one of the biggest commercial impacts was on our customers,” says Stephanie Dunn, Director of Worcestershire-based tree nursery Frank P Matthews. Garden centres were busy watering and looking after the stock they already had, leaving less appetite to take in additional trees in August and delaying some of the nursery’s usual late-summer deliveries. Demand has since picked up strongly, in line with the HTA’s 20% rise in sales of hardy plants, shrubs and trees in September.
The picture was not uniform. Footfall at the nursery’s own Tree Shop did not seem to be affected, helped perhaps by its covered setting and the shade and green backdrop of the trees themselves.
Provender saw the same chain reaction. The end-user caution over watering restrictions that McKenna described led garden centres, garden designers and landscapers to cut back their orders, so a fall in demand at the till travelled straight back to the wholesale nursery.
Gardens and visitor attractions: when and whether people visit
For gardens and visitor attractions, the heat changed when people visited, and whether they came at all.
Across the wider attractions sector, admissions in June were 5% below June 2025, according to the Association for Cultural Enterprises, with declines of around 10% in London, the South East and the Midlands. Gardens, zoos and heritage estates, where visitors spend hours outdoors, are among the most exposed: research associated with Chester Zoo suggests attendance rises with temperature only up to around 21°C.
Waterperry Gardens in Oxfordshire saw a similar pattern. Garden entry tickets in July and August fell to 7,705, from 8,251 a year earlier, a drop of almost 7%. Turnover across the whole site fell by a similar proportion, from £590,758 to £551,000, a shortfall of nearly £40,000 over the two months. Managing Director Simon Buchanan says visitor numbers and turnover have picked up again in September.
The National Garden Scheme reported income 3% down year to date in August, slightly ahead of other garden attractions, which reported falls of around 4–5%. Around 55 NGS gardens cancelled openings over the summer, 11 of them citing the drought. Staff at one National Trust garden told Country Life that its visitor numbers were down by 20,000 by the end of June.
Behind those figures are individual gardens. At Ulting Wick in Essex, which has raised as much as £30,000 a year for the NGS and averages around £25,000, owner Philippa Burrough said many groups had cancelled, and those that did come were smaller than expected. She did not expect this year’s total to match previous years.
Attractions that anticipated the risk fared better. The Eden Project in Cornwall knows that hot, sunny spells draw families to the beach instead, and has built a broader offer in response, from the Eden Sessions concerts to its family programme. This summer it strengthened that programme further and recorded one of its strongest summers in years despite the heat.
Preparing for a hotter climate: business resilience and the costs of inaction
Horticulture has always depended on the weather, but extreme heat and prolonged drought are changing the terms of that relationship. The horticultural calendar has long been built around the seasons, from production schedules and sales peaks to landscape contracts. Planting traditionally took place in autumn and spring to make the most of rainfall and give roots time to establish, and the sector could rely on the rain to do much of the work.
That can no longer be taken for granted. “It’s something we need to wrap our heads around,” says McKenna. “As an industry we can’t keep burying our heads in the sand, hoping it rains tomorrow so we can start planting. Here we are at the end of September and we’ve had only two significant days of rain this month.”
The planting calendar is already shifting, as McKenna’s and Kirkham’s experience shows, and businesses are having to plan around conditions that are less predictable, more disruptive and more costly to manage.
The NHRC’s report argues that record-breaking heat, fire and drought must be treated as a wake-up call. Heat differs from more visible hazards such as floods and storms: its impacts are pervasive, can emerge gradually and are easily underestimated. It also acts as a risk multiplier, compounding drought, wildfire and other climate-related pressures.
For horticulture, the costs are becoming tangible. Earlier declines in spring sales, higher costs of maintaining stock, delayed landscaping projects and uncertainty among customers are putting pressure on margins. The shift in garden centre priorities towards Halloween and Christmas may further squeeze the traditional autumn market for trees and plants.
The result is a growing mismatch between the investment needed to maintain production and the revenue available to fund it. Businesses can change how they operate, but they have far less control over water availability, infrastructure, planning constraints or when customers choose to buy and plant.
That makes adaptation a wider industry and policy challenge. Water security, energy, grid connectivity, planning, land availability and transport infrastructure will increasingly influence whether horticultural businesses can invest, expand production and maintain reliable supply.
Howard Boyd points to recent Green Alliance research on expanding UK fruit and vegetable production, which shows how planning, grid connectivity, water security, land and transport can constrain what growers are able to deliver, and recommends a national spatial strategy because these factors can determine whether individual projects are viable. “Those are not necessarily problems that an individual business can solve on its own,” she says.
“Our members have shown remarkable adaptability, but the conditions have highlighted where investment, infrastructure and policy now need to catch up with the reality of a changing climate,” says Denny. “Importantly, resilience is also commercial. Businesses need confidence to invest in long-term adaptation without being undermined by policy uncertainty or unnecessary regulatory barriers.”
For individual businesses, many of these dependencies lie beyond their control. As the NHRC continues its work, evidence from horticulture can help demonstrate the practical and commercial consequences of extreme heat — and the infrastructure and policy changes needed to enable the sector to adapt.
Have your say
The National Heat Risk Commission is now calling for evidence to help turn the experience of this summer into practical action. It wants to hear from organisations about what worked, what didn’t, and what is needed to make heat preparedness effective and properly funded.
For horticulture, this is an opportunity to be heard. In policy discussions the sector is too often treated as a footnote to agriculture, its contribution overlooked and its concerns left off the table. Evidence from nurseries, growers, garden centres, landscapers and gardens can change that, showing what businesses experienced this summer, from lost sales and delayed projects to rising costs and pressure on water supplies, and the support they need to adapt.
“We particularly want to hear what organisations have already tried, what they have learned and what would make further action possible,” says Howard Boyd.
The call for evidence is open to businesses, public bodies, institutions and voluntary and community organisations across the UK, and closes on 30 October 2026.
The Dutch have spent centuries mastering water. Now a summer of prolonged drought and extreme heat has exposed a very different challenge: how to retain enough freshwater as supplies come increasingly under pressure.

Skip to contentCyclone Arnab: Red alert for Andhra coast as storm set to intensify
HYDERABAD: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a red-message cyclone warning for the Andhra Pradesh and adjoining south Odisha coasts as cyclonic storm Arnab is likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm on October 27.
The storm is expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, close to Yanam, by the forenoon of October 28, with maximum sustained wind speeds of 115–125 kmph and gusts reaching 140 kmph.
Cyclone Arnab moves towards Andhra Pradesh coast
In its National Bulletin No. 10, based on observations at 11.30 am IST on October 26, the IMD said the storm moved nearly westwards at 13 kmph during the preceding six hours.
The cyclonic storm was centred over the west-central and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal near latitude 15.5°N and longitude 88.2°E.
It was located 550 km south-east of Gopalpur in Odisha, 580 km east-south-east of Visakhapatnam, 650 km north-west of Sri Vijaya Puram in the Andaman Islands and 660 km east-south-east of Kakinada.
The storm was also 760 km east-south-east of Machilipatnam and 830 km east-south-east of Bapatla in Andhra Pradesh.
Storm likely to intensify into very severe cyclone
The IMD said Arnab was very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by the evening of October 26.
It is then expected to strengthen into a very severe cyclonic storm over the same region on October 27 before moving northwestwards towards the coast.
Landfall forecast for October 28
The storm is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, close to Yanam, by the forenoon of October 28.
At landfall, the system is expected to have maximum sustained wind speeds of 115–125 kmph, with gusts reaching 140 kmph, according to the bulletin.
